claim: Principal investigators at-large do not have equal access to federal grant funding for scientific research.
source: Principal investigators at-large do not have equal access to federal grant funding for scientific research and this chronic problem has long been recognized by federal funding agencies (National Academies, 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to National Academies, 2013

claim: There are disparities in grant application success rates or award sizes or both for investigators grouped by race.
source: There are disparities in grant application success rates or award sizes or both for investigators grouped by race (Ginther et al., 2011)
evidence: Supported by citation to Ginther et al., 2011

claim: There are disparities in grant application success rates or award sizes or both for investigators grouped by gender.
source: There are disparities in grant application success rates or award sizes or both for investigators grouped by race (Ginther et al., 2011), gender (Pohlhaus et al., 2011; Magua et al., 2017)
evidence: Supported by citations to Pohlhaus et al., 2011 and Magua et al., 2017

claim: There are disparities in grant application success rates or award sizes or both for investigators grouped by age.
source: There are disparities in grant application success rates or award sizes or both for investigators grouped by race (Ginther et al., 2011), gender (Pohlhaus et al., 2011; Magua et al., 2017), age (Levitt and Levitt, 2017)
evidence: Supported by citation to Levitt and Levitt, 2017

claim: There are disparities in grant application success rates or award sizes or both for investigators grouped by institution.
source: There are disparities in grant application success rates or award sizes or both for investigators grouped by race (Ginther et al., 2011), gender (Pohlhaus et al., 2011; Magua et al., 2017), age (Levitt and Levitt, 2017), institution (Murray et al., 2016)
evidence: Supported by citation to Murray et al., 2016

claim: There are disparities in grant application success rates or award sizes or both for investigators grouped by state.
source: There are disparities in grant application success rates or award sizes or both for investigators grouped by race (Ginther et al., 2011), gender (Pohlhaus et al., 2011; Magua et al., 2017), age (Levitt and Levitt, 2017), institution (Murray et al., 2016) and state (Wahls, 2016a).
evidence: Supported by citation to Wahls, 2016a

claim: Disparities in funding persist even after controlling for other factors.
source: To the extent tested these disparities persist even after controlling for other factors, suggesting that implicit (subconscious) biases and social prestige mechanisms (e.g., the Matthew effect) can affect allocations of funding.
evidence: Based on inference from the persistence of disparities after controlling for confounding factors

claim: Implicit biases and social prestige mechanisms can affect allocations of funding.
source: To the extent tested these disparities persist even after controlling for other factors, suggesting that implicit (subconscious) biases and social prestige mechanisms (e.g., the Matthew effect) can affect allocations of funding.
evidence: Speculative inference based on persistence of disparities

claim: Unbalanced allocations of funding are detrimental to the biomedical research enterprise in the US.
source: However, we do not need to define the various potential sources of bias, or even accept that there might be any bias at all in funding decisions, to understand that the unbalanced allocations of funding are detrimental to the biomedical research enterprise in the US.
evidence: Based on logical inference from the analysis presented in the manuscript

claim: 1% of NIH-funded investigators get 11% of research project grant dollars.
source: Just 1% of NIH-funded investigators get 11% of research project grant dollars and 40% of the money goes to 10% of funded investigators (Collins, 2017a; amounts of funding include administrative supplements, if any).
evidence: Supported by citation to Collins, 2017a

claim: 40% of research project grant money goes to 10% of funded investigators.
source: Just 1% of NIH-funded investigators get 11% of research project grant dollars and 40% of the money goes to 10% of funded investigators (Collins, 2017a; amounts of funding include administrative supplements, if any).
evidence: Supported by citation to Collins, 2017a

claim: The NIH gives half of all research project grant dollars to about 19% of funded investigators.
source: While the NIH gives half of all research project grant dollars to about 19% of funded investigators, half the money goes to just 2% of funded organizations and 10% of states (Figure 1).
evidence: Supported by reference to Figure 1

claim: Half of NIH research project grant money goes to just 2% of funded organizations.
source: While the NIH gives half of all research project grant dollars to about 19% of funded investigators, half the money goes to just 2% of funded organizations and 10% of states (Figure 1).
evidence: Supported by reference to Figure 1

claim: Half of NIH research project grant money goes to 10% of states.
source: While the NIH gives half of all research project grant dollars to about 19% of funded investigators, half the money goes to just 2% of funded organizations and 10% of states (Figure 1).
evidence: Supported by reference to Figure 1

claim: Funding inequality has been rising since 1985.
source: Such "funding inequality has been rising since 1985, with a small segment of investigators and institutes getting an increasing proportion of funds, and investigators who start in the top funding ranks tend to stay there (which results in stasis, or lack of mobility)" (Katz and Matter, 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Katz and Matter, 2017

claim: A small segment of investigators and institutes are getting an increasing proportion of funds.
source: Such "funding inequality has been rising since 1985, with a small segment of investigators and institutes getting an increasing proportion of funds, and investigators who start in the top funding ranks tend to stay there (which results in stasis, or lack of mobility)" (Katz and Matter, 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Katz and Matter, 2017

claim: Investigators who start in the top funding ranks tend to stay there.
source: Such "funding inequality has been rising since 1985, with a small segment of investigators and institutes getting an increasing proportion of funds, and investigators who start in the top funding ranks tend to stay there (which results in stasis, or lack of mobility)" (Katz and Matter, 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Katz and Matter, 2017

claim: Increasing hyper-competition for limited resources places the majority of awardees at risk of laboratory closure when they lose their sole NIH grant.
source: Elsewhere in the ranks, increasing hyper-competition for the limited resources places the majority of awardees at risk of laboratory closure when they lose their sole NIH grant (Peifer, 2017a).
evidence: Supported by citation to Peifer, 2017a

claim: Hyper-competition serves as an effective barrier for the recruitment of young investigators into the biomedical workforce.
source: The hyper-competition also serves as an effective barrier for the recruitment of young investigators into the biomedical workforce, causing many highly talented trainees and early career scientists to redirect their career paths away from working on the underlying biology, diagnosis and treatment of human diseases (Carr, 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Carr, 2013

claim: Hyper-competition causes many highly talented trainees and early career scientists to redirect their career paths away from working on the underlying biology, diagnosis and treatment of human diseases.
source: The hyper-competition also serves as an effective barrier for the recruitment of young investigators into the biomedical workforce, causing many highly talented trainees and early career scientists to redirect their career paths away from working on the underlying biology, diagnosis and treatment of human diseases (Carr, 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Carr, 2013

claim: Thought-leaders and organizations such as the Federation of American Societies for Experimental Biology have advocated for a more equitable distribution of funding to help sustain the biomedical research enterprise.
source: Consequently, thought-leaders and organizations such as the Federation of American Societies for Experimental Biology have advocated for a more equitable distribution of funding to help sustain the biomedical research enterprise (Alberts et al., 2014; Lorsch, 2015; FASEB, 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Alberts et al., 2014; Lorsch, 2015; FASEB, 2015

claim: Underfunding and non-funding of some groups of scientists compromises their ability to contribute effectively to the missions of the NIH.
source: At population scale, the underfunding and non-funding of some groups of scientists (the majority) compromises their ability to contribute effectively to the missions of the NIH.
evidence: Based on logical inference from the analysis of funding disparities

claim: A more balanced distribution of resources among investigators would strengthen the diversity of the research ecosystem, increase the likelihood of scientific breakthroughs, and lead to a greater return on taxpayers' investments.
source: It has been posited that a more balanced distribution of resources among investigators—geared towards harnessing the greatest possible number of perspectives, creative ideas and experimental approaches—would strengthen the diversity of the research ecosystem, increase the likelihood of scientific breakthroughs, and lead to a greater return on taxpayers' investments (Lorsch, 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Lorsch, 2015

claim: Individual investigators each have a finite capacity to carry out grant-related duties.
source: In his 1985 commentary in Cell, Bruce Alberts pointed out that individual investigators each have a finite capacity to carry out grant-related duties and that their productivity falls when their amounts of funding exceed those capacity limits: consequently, highly funded laboratories are generally "less productive" and represent a "poor training environment" relative to more-modestly funded laboratories.
evidence: Supported by reference to Alberts' 1985 commentary

claim: Investigator productivity falls when their amounts of funding exceed their capacity limits.
source: In his 1985 commentary in Cell, Bruce Alberts pointed out that individual investigators each have a finite capacity to carry out grant-related duties and that their productivity falls when their amounts of funding exceed those capacity limits: consequently, highly funded laboratories are generally "less productive" and represent a "poor training environment" relative to more-modestly funded laboratories.
evidence: Supported by reference to Alberts' 1985 commentary

claim: Highly funded laboratories are generally less productive relative to more-modestly funded laboratories.
source: In his 1985 commentary in Cell, Bruce Alberts pointed out that individual investigators each have a finite capacity to carry out grant-related duties and that their productivity falls when their amounts of funding exceed those capacity limits: consequently, highly funded laboratories are generally "less productive" and represent a "poor training environment" relative to more-modestly funded laboratories.
evidence: Supported by reference to Alberts' 1985 commentary

claim: Highly funded laboratories represent a poor training environment relative to more-modestly funded laboratories.
source: In his 1985 commentary in Cell, Bruce Alberts pointed out that individual investigators each have a finite capacity to carry out grant-related duties and that their productivity falls when their amounts of funding exceed those capacity limits: consequently, highly funded laboratories are generally "less productive" and represent a "poor training environment" relative to more-modestly funded laboratories.
evidence: Supported by reference to Alberts' 1985 commentary

claim: Bruce Alberts advocated for capping the total amount of funding that each investigator can receive.
source: Alberts advocated for capping the total amount of funding that each investigator can receive, explaining how this would reduce waste and would permit the funding of more investigators, thereby increasing the diversity and net productivity of the research enterprise (Alberts, 1985).
evidence: Supported by citation to Alberts, 1985

claim: Capping funding per investigator would reduce waste and permit the funding of more investigators, thereby increasing the diversity and net productivity of the research enterprise.
source: Alberts advocated for capping the total amount of funding that each investigator can receive, explaining how this would reduce waste and would permit the funding of more investigators, thereby increasing the diversity and net productivity of the research enterprise (Alberts, 1985).
evidence: Supported by citation to Alberts, 1985

claim: Scientific output does not scale uniformly with amounts of funding.
source: About three decades later, that prescient insight was validated by a series of empirical studies which showed that scientific output, as measured in multiple ways, does not scale uniformly with amounts of funding and that there are diminishing marginal (incremental) returns on investments in research (see, for example, Mongeon et al., 2016 and references therein).
evidence: Supported by citation to Mongeon et al., 2016 and references therein

claim: There are diminishing marginal returns on investments in research.
source: About three decades later, that prescient insight was validated by a series of empirical studies which showed that scientific output, as measured in multiple ways, does not scale uniformly with amounts of funding and that there are diminishing marginal (incremental) returns on investments in research (see, for example, Mongeon et al., 2016 and references therein).
evidence: Supported by citation to Mongeon et al., 2016 and references therein

claim: Diminishing marginal returns apply for the heavily skewed allocations of NIH funding among individual grants.
source: These diminishing marginal returns apply for the heavily skewed allocations of NIH funding among individual grants (Lauer, 2016a), investigators (Lauer et al., 2017), institutions (Wahls, 2016) and quartiles of states (Wahls, 2016a).
evidence: Supported by citation to Lauer, 2016a

claim: Diminishing marginal returns apply for the heavily skewed allocations of NIH funding among investigators.
source: These diminishing marginal returns apply for the heavily skewed allocations of NIH funding among individual grants (Lauer, 2016a), investigators (Lauer et al., 2017), institutions (Wahls, 2016) and quartiles of states (Wahls, 2016a).
evidence: Supported by citation to Lauer et al., 2017

claim: Diminishing marginal returns apply for the heavily skewed allocations of NIH funding among institutions.
source: These diminishing marginal returns apply for the heavily skewed allocations of NIH funding among individual grants (Lauer, 2016a), investigators (Lauer et al., 2017), institutions (Wahls, 2016) and quartiles of states (Wahls, 2016a).
evidence: Supported by citation to Wahls, 2016

claim: Diminishing marginal returns apply for the heavily skewed allocations of NIH funding among quartiles of states.
source: These diminishing marginal returns apply for the heavily skewed allocations of NIH funding among individual grants (Lauer, 2016a), investigators (Lauer et al., 2017), institutions (Wahls, 2016) and quartiles of states (Wahls, 2016a).
evidence: Supported by citation to Wahls, 2016a

claim: Giving a disproportionately large share of grant funding to a minority of investigators, institutions and states is counterproductive.
source: Giving a disproportionately large share of grant funding to a minority of investigators, institutions and states is counterproductive—whether or not the imbalances are driven by bias.
evidence: Based on inference from the data on diminishing marginal returns

claim: In May 2017 the NIH director Francis Collins announced a new policy to cap funding per investigator.
source: In response to the plethora of data from groups within and outside of the NIH, in May 2017 the NIH director Francis Collins announced a new policy to cap funding per investigator (Collins, 2017a).
evidence: Supported by citation to Collins, 2017a

claim: The May 2017 NIH policy would have capped the number of research awards at three R01 grant equivalents per investigator.
source: This was a modest plan that would have capped the number of research awards (three R01 grant equivalents), not dollars, per investigator.
evidence: Based on description of the announced policy

claim: Only about one in five of the investigators with more than a million dollars of NIH research project grant funding per year has more than three such grants.
source: The majority of very well-funded investigators would have been protected from the caps because only about one in five of the investigators with more than a million dollars of NIH research project grant funding per year has more than three such grants (Wahls, 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Wahls, 2017

claim: The May 2017 NIH policy would have freed up enough funds for about 1,600 new awards to help early and mid-career researchers who just miss the pay line for funding.
source: Nevertheless, according to Collins, the new policy would have freed up enough funds for about 1,600 new awards to help early and mid-career researchers who just miss the pay line for funding (Collins, 2017a).
evidence: Supported by citation to Collins, 2017a

claim: The NIH supports almost 50,000 competitive grants to researchers.
source: The "about 1,600 new awards" might seem like an impressive number, but it is actually a trivial increase given that the NIH supports almost 50,000 competitive grants to researchers.
evidence: Based on knowledge of NIH grant portfolio

claim: In June 2017, the NIH cancelled its incipient policy on funding caps.
source: One month later, in a stunning about-face that ignored the unanimity of conclusions from studies conducted within and outside of the NIH, the NIH cancelled the incipient policy on funding caps (Collins, 2017b).
evidence: Supported by citation to Collins, 2017b

claim: The cancelled funding cap policy was replaced by the Next Generation Researchers Initiative (NGRI).
source: It was replaced by a plan (the Next Generation Researchers Initiative, or NGRI) that is predicted to, over five years, support up to 2,000 additional investigators (Collins, 2017b).
evidence: Supported by citation to Collins, 2017b

claim: The NGRI plan is predicted to support up to 2,000 additional investigators over five years.
source: It was replaced by a plan (the Next Generation Researchers Initiative, or NGRI) that is predicted to, over five years, support up to 2,000 additional investigators (Collins, 2017b).
evidence: Supported by citation to Collins, 2017b

claim: The NGRI plan has no provisions to address the inefficient utilization of research dollars caused by the focused concentrations of funding.
source: The NGRI plan has no provisions to address the inefficient utilization of research dollars caused by the focused concentrations of funding at any of the levels described above.
evidence: Based on analysis of the NGRI plan

claim: Each dollar of direct costs corresponds to about $1.50 of total costs.
source: For those unfamiliar with the difference, each dollar of direct costs corresponds to about $1.50 of total costs (direct costs plus indirect costs).
evidence: Based on established knowledge of NIH grant cost structure

claim: Total costs provide the most appropriate parameter when it comes to measuring returns on taxpayers' investments.
source: Although indirect cost rates vary between institutions, both direct costs and indirect costs go to support the research of a given project, so total costs provide the most appropriate parameter when it comes to measuring returns on taxpayers' investments.
evidence: Based on logical reasoning about cost accounting

claim: Scientific output for NIGMS-funded investigators tapers off above $300,000 of annual direct costs.
source: One study reported that scientific output for investigators funded by the NIH's National Institute of General Medical Sciences (NIGMS), based on the number of grant-weighted publications and citation rates, tapers off above $300,000 of annual direct costs and diminishes further thereafter, "with only small discontinuous increase above $500,000" (Basson et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Basson et al., 2016

claim: Funding for a first R01 grant ($200,000 annual direct costs) to an investigator produces, on average, about five publications during the funding period.
source: Funding for a first R01 grant ($200,000 annual direct costs) to an investigator produces, on average, about five publications during the funding period, whereas the same amount of funding for a third R01 grant yields only about one additional publication (Lorsch, 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Lorsch, 2015

claim: The same amount of funding for a third R01 grant yields only about one additional publication.
source: Funding for a first R01 grant ($200,000 annual direct costs) to an investigator produces, on average, about five publications during the funding period, whereas the same amount of funding for a third R01 grant yields only about one additional publication (Lorsch, 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Lorsch, 2015

claim: About 80% of the dollars allocated for each third grant to an investigator are not being used productively, relative to what could be realized by giving that grant to an unfunded investigator.
source: At least at population scale, about 80% of the dollars allocated for each third grant to an investigator are not being used productively, relative to what could be realized by giving that grant to an unfunded investigator (of which there are many, given that about three quarters of applicants are denied funding each year; Rockey, 2014).
evidence: Based on inference from the productivity data and citation to Rockey, 2014

claim: About three quarters of NIH grant applicants are denied funding each year.
source: At least at population scale, about 80% of the dollars allocated for each third grant to an investigator are not being used productively, relative to what could be realized by giving that grant to an unfunded investigator (of which there are many, given that about three quarters of applicants are denied funding each year; Rockey, 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Rockey, 2014

claim: Optimal rates of output occur at about $400,000 of total costs per investigator.
source: Optimal rates of output, based on time-normalized, field-normalized citation impact factors, occur at about $400,000 of total costs per investigator (the sweet spot for funding; Figure 2).
evidence: Supported by reference to Figure 2 and the analysis described

claim: The sweet spot for funding coincides almost exactly with median funding per investigator.
source: That sweet spot coincides almost exactly with median funding per investigator (Figure 1).
evidence: Supported by reference to Figure 1

claim: There are diminishing marginal returns for amounts of funding above and below the sweet spot.
source: However, there are diminishing marginal returns for amounts of funding above and below that sweet spot.
evidence: Based on the analysis of productivity data

claim: The incremental returns for each dollar of funding at $800,000 are about 25% to 40% of the returns at the sweet spot.
source: For example, the incremental returns for each dollar of funding at $800,000 (twice the optimal level) and at $200,000 (half the optimal level) are about 25% to 40% of the returns at the sweet spot (Figure 2).
evidence: Supported by reference to Figure 2

claim: The incremental returns for each dollar of funding at $200,000 are about 25% to 40% of the returns at the sweet spot.
source: For example, the incremental returns for each dollar of funding at $800,000 (twice the optimal level) and at $200,000 (half the optimal level) are about 25% to 40% of the returns at the sweet spot (Figure 2).
evidence: Supported by reference to Figure 2

claim: The diminishing marginal returns persist even when award data are parsed by NIH institute.
source: Notably, the diminishing marginal returns persist even when award data are parsed by NIH institute, for "elite" investigators, and by human versus non-human model systems (Lauer et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Lauer et al., 2017

claim: The diminishing marginal returns persist even for elite investigators.
source: Notably, the diminishing marginal returns persist even when award data are parsed by NIH institute, for "elite" investigators, and by human versus non-human model systems (Lauer et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Lauer et al., 2017

claim: The diminishing marginal returns persist when data are parsed by human versus non-human model systems.
source: Notably, the diminishing marginal returns persist even when award data are parsed by NIH institute, for "elite" investigators, and by human versus non-human model systems (Lauer et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Lauer et al., 2017

claim: A cap of one million dollars of annual NIH research project grant funding per investigator would free up enough money to support about 10,000 additional investigators.
source: For example, a cap of one million dollars (total costs) of annual NIH research project grant funding per investigator—which is an extremely generous amount of support that is far beyond the point at which diminishing marginal returns kick in (see Figure 2)—would reduce inefficiencies at the top end of the funding distribution and would free up enough money to support about 10,000 additional investigators (Wahls, 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Wahls, 2017

claim: Investigators with amounts of NIH funding below the sweet spot have sub-optimal productivity.
source: Notably, investigators with amounts of NIH funding below the sweet spot also have sub-optimal productivity (Figure 2; Lauer et al., 2017), presumably because they lack the critical mass (e.g., number of grant-supported personnel) to sustain high productivity.
evidence: Supported by reference to Figure 2 and citation to Lauer et al., 2017

claim: Investigators with funding below the sweet spot lack the critical mass to sustain high productivity.
source: Notably, investigators with amounts of NIH funding below the sweet spot also have sub-optimal productivity (Figure 2; Lauer et al., 2017), presumably because they lack the critical mass (e.g., number of grant-supported personnel) to sustain high productivity.
evidence: Speculative inference about the cause of sub-optimal productivity

claim: A lower limit of $200,000 and an upper limit of $800,000 total costs would be appropriate for NIH research project grant funding per awardee.
source: I posit, based on available data (such as Figure 2) and as a point for discussion, that a lower limit of $200,000 and an upper limit of $800,000 total costs would be appropriate.
evidence: Based on inference from the productivity data in Figure 2

claim: Within the proposed funding range, median funding per investigator would still be close to the productivity sweet spot of $400,000.
source: Within this range, median funding per investigator would still be close to the productivity sweet spot of $400,000 (Figure 1).
evidence: Supported by reference to Figure 1

claim: The proposed funding limits would free up enough money to support more than 10,000 additional investigators, each funded at the productivity sweet spot of $400,000.
source: Moreover, these specific limits would free up enough money to support more than 10,000 additional investigators, each funded at (or with mean funding at) the productivity sweet spot of $400,000.
evidence: Based on calculations presented in the manuscript

claim: In FY2015, 5,038 research project grant recipients each got more than $800,000.
source: Based on FY2015 values from NIH RePORTER, 5,038 research project grant recipients (which is 20% of the total number of grant recipients) each got more than $800,000.
evidence: Based on data from NIH RePORTER database

claim: 5,038 research project grant recipients represent 20% of the total number of grant recipients in FY2015.
source: Based on FY2015 values from NIH RePORTER, 5,038 research project grant recipients (which is 20% of the total number of grant recipients) each got more than $800,000.
evidence: Based on data from NIH RePORTER database

claim: The 5,038 investigators who each received more than $800,000 together received about $8.39 billion in FY2015.
source: Together they received about $8.39 billion, so limiting each to $800,000 would free up about $4.36 billion.
evidence: Based on data from NIH RePORTER database

claim: Limiting each of the 5,038 highly-funded investigators to $800,000 would free up about $4.36 billion.
source: Together they received about $8.39 billion, so limiting each to $800,000 would free up about $4.36 billion.
evidence: Based on calculation from NIH RePORTER data

claim: In FY2015, there were 2,302 investigators with funding between $10,000 and $199,999.
source: There were 2,302 investigators (9% of the total) with funding between $10,000 and $199,999.
evidence: Based on data from NIH RePORTER database

claim: 2,302 investigators with funding between $10,000 and $199,999 represent 9% of the total number of grant recipients in FY2015.
source: There were 2,302 investigators (9% of the total) with funding between $10,000 and $199,999.
evidence: Based on data from NIH RePORTER database

claim: The 2,302 investigators with funding between $10,000 and $199,999 together got $0.32 billion in FY2015.
source: Together those awardees got $0.32 billion, so bringing each of them up to the $200,000 minimum would cost about $0.14 billion.

claim: Bringing each of the 2,302 low-funded investigators up to the $200,000 minimum would cost about $0.14 billion.
source: Together those awardees got $0.32 billion, so bringing each of them up to the $200,000 minimum would cost about $0.14 billion.
evidence: Based on calculation from NIH RePORTER data

claim: The minimum and maximum funding limits would free up about $4.22 billion.
source: Thus the minimum and maximum funding limits would free up about $4.22 billion, which is enough to award $400,000 to each of 10,542 additional investigators who do not have funding.
evidence: Based on calculation from NIH RePORTER data

claim: $4.22 billion is enough to award $400,000 to each of 10,542 additional investigators who do not have funding.
source: Thus the minimum and maximum funding limits would free up about $4.22 billion, which is enough to award $400,000 to each of 10,542 additional investigators who do not have funding.
evidence: Based on calculation from NIH RePORTER data

claim: The number of NIH research project grant applicants rose from about 60,000 to slightly less than 90,000 between 2003 and 2015.
source: When measured over five-year periods ending in 2003 and 2015, the number of NIH research project grant applicants rose from about 60,000 to slightly less than 90,000, but the number of awardees held steady at about 27,500 (Lauer, 2016b).
evidence: Supported by citation to Lauer, 2016b

claim: The number of NIH research project grant awardees held steady at about 27,500 between 2003 and 2015.
source: When measured over five-year periods ending in 2003 and 2015, the number of NIH research project grant applicants rose from about 60,000 to slightly less than 90,000, but the number of awardees held steady at about 27,500 (Lauer, 2016b).
evidence: Supported by citation to Lauer, 2016b

claim: The NIH budget lost 22% of its purchasing power between 2003 and 2015 due to budget cuts, sequestration and inflation.
source: Over the same time frame (2003 to 2015), the value of the NIH budget not only failed to keep pace with the expanding US population in general, and the expanding scientific workforce in particular, it actually lost 22% of its purchasing power due to budget cuts, sequestration and inflation (FASEB, 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to FASEB, 2017

claim: Grant application success rates and investigator funding rates have fallen fairly steadily over time.
source: For these reasons, grant application success rates and investigator funding rates have fallen fairly steadily over time.
evidence: Based on inference from the data on applicant numbers and budget constraints

claim: Each year only about one quarter of NIH grant applicants get funded.
source: Each year only about one quarter of applicants, including those who submit multiple proposals, get funded (Rockey, 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Rockey, 2014

claim: Less than one third of NIH grant applicants secure any research project grant funding over a five-year period.
source: Similarly, less than one third of applicants secure any research project grant funding over a five-year period (up to 2015); about 60,000 applicants do not get any of their applications funded (Lauer, 2016b).
evidence: Supported by citation to Lauer, 2016b

claim: About 60,000 NIH grant applicants do not get any of their applications funded over a five-year period.
source: Similarly, less than one third of applicants secure any research project grant funding over a five-year period (up to 2015); about 60,000 applicants do not get any of their applications funded (Lauer, 2016b).
evidence: Supported by citation to Lauer, 2016b

claim: The unutilized capacity of the biomedical workforce is large enough to sustain an additional 10,500 awardees.
source: Therefore, the unutilized capacity of the biomedical workforce (as measured by unfunded applicants) is large enough to sustain an additional 10,500 awardees, which would increase the pool of funded investigators by about 38%.
evidence: Based on inference from the data on unfunded applicants

claim: Supporting an additional 10,500 awardees would increase the pool of funded investigators by about 38%.
source: Therefore, the unutilized capacity of the biomedical workforce (as measured by unfunded applicants) is large enough to sustain an additional 10,500 awardees, which would increase the pool of funded investigators by about 38%.
evidence: Based on calculation from the data on current awardees

claim: Dollar-based funding limits would be insufficient in isolation to address the problem of too many investigators competing for too few research dollars.
source: It thus seems clear that while dollar-based funding limits would be quite effective at harnessing additional talent, in isolation they would be insufficient to address the problem of too many investigators competing for too few research dollars.
evidence: Based on inference from the analysis of the biomedical workforce capacity

claim: Restoring the NIH budget to its inflation-adjusted 2003 levels or higher would be required to ensure that biomedical research in the US remains competitive on the international stage.
source: Additional steps, such as restoring the NIH budget to its inflation-adjusted 2003 levels or even higher (to account for population expansion), would be required to ensure that biomedical research in the US remains competitive on the international stage.
evidence: Based on inference from the analysis of budget constraints

claim: The MIRA program seeks to increase the efficiency of funding by providing investigators with greater stability and flexibility while distributing funding more widely among investigators.
source: The MIRA program seeks to increase the efficiency of funding by providing investigators with greater stability and flexibility while distributing funding more widely among investigators.
evidence: Based on description of the MIRA program

claim: MIRA awardees must agree to accept the MIRA grant as their sole source of NIGMS research funding.
source: To participate in this program, MIRA awardees must agree to accept the MIRA grant as their sole source of NIGMS research funding.
evidence: Based on description of MIRA program requirements

claim: The MIRA program, coupled with clearly defined limits on dollars of support per investigator, could serve as a paradigm for all NIH research project grant funding.
source: The MIRA program, coupled with clearly defined limits on dollars of support per investigator, could serve as a paradigm for all NIH research project grant funding.
evidence: Speculative proposal based on the analysis presented

claim: Congress began restoring the NIH budget in FY2016.
source: Congress began restoring the NIH budget in FY2016 (FASEB, 2017) and all of us should encourage them to keep doing so.
evidence: Supported by citation to FASEB, 2017

claim: Policies aimed at sustaining the biomedical research enterprise will be most effective only if they address adequately the vast disparities in funding among investigators, institutions and states.
